claims.text: Refining a eutectic microstructure increases its interphase lamellar-boundary area or density.
Increased interphase-boundary area creates localized galvanic couples.
Increased interphase-boundary area creates stress-concentration sites.
Interphase boundaries are preferentially damaged during simultaneous elevated-temperature wear and corrosion.
Preferential boundary damage rapidly exposes chemically heterogeneous interfaces.
Exposure of chemically heterogeneous interfaces synergistically accelerates overall degradation.
A coarse eutectic spacing produces fewer interphase boundaries than a refined eutectic spacing.
Controlled heat treatment using annealing and rapid quenching can vary eutectic spacing and interphase-boundary density.
Chemical heterogeneity at interphase interfaces causes localized galvanic corrosion.
Interphase interfaces focus stresses generated by mechanical wear.
Preferential removal of boundary material exposes fresh reactive surfaces to the corrosive environment.
Fresh-surface exposure accelerates both wear and corrosion through a synergistic mechanism.
Relative to a coarse-spacing baseline, the refined microstructure will exhibit higher localized corrosion rates at interphase boundaries.
Relative to a coarse-spacing baseline, the refined microstructure will exhibit greater wear damage at interphase boundaries.
The refined microstructure will undergo greater total degradation than the coarse-spacing baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate under oxidizing conditions at 350–400 °C and constant sliding load.
Heat treatment may also change phase stability or defect density, potentially confounding the effect of interphase-boundary area.
The proposed controlled comparison uses compositionally identical samples that differ only in eutectic spacing and interphase-boundary area.
Failure of the refined sample to show significantly higher localized corrosion and boundary wear than the coarse sample would falsify the proposed boundary-driven explanation.
